BARCELONA, Spain — Automakers are exploring more integrated in-cabin sensing architectures, combining cameras and radars to monitor drivers and passengers.

The trend comes as European safety assessments place greater emphasis on driver monitoring and occupant safety, including the detection of children left in vehicles.

At the AutoSens Europe 2026 conference in Barcelona, Davide Maggi, project officer at the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre (JRC), argued that automakers are consolidating these separate sensing tasks into unified central systems to meet five-star safety rating criteria without incurring the prohibitive costs of installing multiple optical cameras throughout the vehicle cabin.

Replacing the steering-column sensor

For nearly a decade, automotive safety engineers have addressed driver distraction by placing optical sensors directly behind the steering wheel. That placement provides a direct, unobstructed view of the driver’s eyes and face, letting algorithms detect blinking, gaze shifts, and signs of fatigue.

“Ten years ago, when we started seeing the first driver monitoring systems, they were all steering column-based—most of them, except for Tesla, which was the only one adding an RGB camera in the center top,” Maggi told EE Times during an interview at AutoSens.

That dedicated architecture is rapidly losing ground as car companies seek to streamline interior electronics and reduce component counts. Instead of positioning a single camera aimed exclusively at the driver, manufacturers are moving toward centralized optical sensors mounted near the rearview mirror or embedded within the center dashboard display to cover the driver and passengers simultaneously.

“It seems like everyone is moving away from a driver monitoring system just facing the driver and pointing toward a camera in the center,” Maggi said. He noted that a single centrally mounted device “can also provide both driver monitoring and occupant monitoring across the entire front and rear cabin.”

Central cameras involve optical tradeoffs

Consolidating two separate sensing functions into a single central camera involves technical compromises. Moving an optical sensor from the steering column to the center of the vehicle creates a more oblique viewing angle, making it harder to track subtle facial movements when the driver turns away.

Maggi described the engineering challenge with a spatial metaphor. “Having the camera up there and moving from a two-camera system—one for DMS and one for occupant monitoring—to one that does both has its own challenges,” he said. “The blanket is this size: If you pull it from one side, some other part will go uncovered.“

In practice, a central mounting point leaves optical algorithms vulnerable to line-of-sight obstructions. “In this case, if you put the camera up there, whenever you lose accuracy in tracking where the driver is looking when he moves his head to this side, basically half of the face is gone,” Maggi said. He added that everyday driver’s clothing and accessories can introduce further interference, noting that “with the headwear, it could be getting tricky, because if you’re wearing a hat or anything, some blockage might occur.“

Optical sensors also face physical limitations when detecting passengers obscured from view, such as an infant sleeping under a heavy blanket or positioned below the camera’s line of sight.

Combining cameras and radars

To overcome the visual blind spots of a single central camera without adding secondary optical assemblies, vehicle suppliers combine central cameras with in-cabin radars, Maggi said. Short-range millimeter-wave radar and ultra-wideband sensing systems can detect subtle movements, including a sleeping child’s breathing, even through fabrics and other materials.

“It’s interesting that now it’s going back to having one-size-fits-all from a technology side,” Maggi said regarding the move toward centralized cabin architectures. “And the new part is that most of them—actually, I think all of them—are also embedding radar monitoring systems to detect what the camera cannot see.“

By pairing a single central camera with radars, Tier 1 automotive suppliers can support both driver monitoring and child presence detection. At the conference, system developers demonstrated various integration approaches, combining visual video feeds with real-time radar point-cloud data.

Maggi highlighted the cost advantages of this hybrid architecture for volume vehicle production. “I’ve seen some of them already providing a high-level vision combining camera and radar; others just provide a visual of what they get from the point-cloud data,” he said. “It’s fascinating. It’s supposed to be a lot cheaper than mounting cameras to monitor everything.“

Regulatory pressure and Euro NCAP ratings

The acceleration toward merged in-cabin sensing systems is closely tied to updated European vehicle safety assessment criteria. The European New Car Assessment Programme, known as Euro NCAP, has introduced expanded protocols for 2026 and outlined further changes for 2029 that evaluate driver state monitoring, driver impairment detection, and child presence detection.

Maggi, whose work at the Joint Research Centre involves embedding human factors principles into European regulatory frameworks, emphasized the influence of these ratings on engineering decisions.

“For sure, cost is one thing,” Maggi said. “I don’t know what influence that Euro NCAP has had in these choices, because now in Euro NCAP you can see that for 2026 and 2029 you have more requirements for driver monitoring and occupant monitoring especially, which was not there some years ago.“

Because Euro NCAP ratings are important to European car buyers when selecting new vehicles, automakers prioritize meeting these test criteria efficiently over deploying elaborate, proprietary monitoring hardware.

“I don’t know if manufacturers now see that there’s no profitability in having a high-end driver monitoring system,” Maggi noted. ”Because the only thing that matters is actually getting five stars on Euro NCAP.” 

Separating assistance from autonomous driving

Maggi explained that European authorities are setting clearer regulatory boundaries between driver-assistance features and fully automated driving systems. 

To prevent driver confusion regarding vehicle capabilities, European regulations strictly separate driver control assistance systems (DCAS) from automated driving systems (ADS).

“Regulatory-wise, the first thing that we tried to do is to separate levels of automation as they are defining a level, completely discarding the SAE [levels of driving automation] definition and really going into the details of what is an ADS and how it should be regulated, versus what is an assistant system,” Maggi explained.

Under these regulatory guidelines, automated systems cannot abruptly transfer control into driver-assistance modes. “DCAS regulation and ADS regulation are two very separate things,” Maggi said. He added that automated regulations specify “that there cannot be a transition from a Level 4 system to a Level 2 system, to avoid any more confusion happening with the driver not knowing the capability of the system in the vehicle.“

Following our initial coverage of the Delaware federal jury verdict in the Qualcomm and Arm dispute, Arm contacted EE Times to clarify the IP vendor’s position. In a phone interview with EE Times, Arm CMO Ami Badani discussed the company’s stance on the jury’s decision and the stakes surrounding licensing negotiations for Arm’s next-generation v10 architecture. 

Badani contended that Arm emerged as a “victor” in court due to the nominal $2 damages award and the presiding judge’s reluctance to oversee future licensing terms, while emphasizing the ongoing technical and commercial collaboration with Qualcomm.

She also commented on the rise of other architectures such as RISC-V, as experts caution that restrictive proprietary frameworks may compel semiconductor designers toward open standards to meet the demands of evolving AI workloads.

Arm characterizes nominal damages and judicial limits as victory

Badani, who attended several proceedings in Wilmington, argued that the jury’s decision to award Qualcomm just $2 in nominal damages supports Arm’s position. The jury awarded $1 for a licensing breach and $1 for interference with Qualcomm’s business relationship with Meta, while finding for Arm on other allegations.

She argued that the minimal financial penalty supported Arm’s position that it operated in good faith throughout its licensing relationship with Qualcomm and that its conduct did not warrant substantial monetary damages.

Badani cited recent Bloomberg reporting on closing arguments in the case before U.S. District Judge Maryellen Noreika. During the hearing, Judge Noreika expressed strong reservations about Qualcomm’s request for the court to compel Arm to negotiate in good faith new licensing terms for its upcoming v10 architecture.

The judge characterized Qualcomm’s bid for judicial oversight of commercial terms as “very, very drastic,” remarking that the court would not step in to regulate Arm’s business practices or act as a regulatory supervisor.

Furthermore, Badani cited the court’s reluctance to dictate contractual rates or grant additional financial remedies as further support for Arm’s position. She also indicated that a final written ruling on the remaining antitrust and licensing claims could take several weeks, as both corporate parties complete their final written submissions for judicial review.

Despite the four-year court battle, Badani emphasized that Arm and Qualcomm maintain ongoing technical and commercial collaboration. She noted that, in Arm’s view, Qualcomm is not actively seeking further monetary compensation, but rather attempting to maximize the commercial and technical value derived from its ongoing licensing relationship.

Traction for RISC-V

Badani also directly addressed industry analysis suggesting that open-standard instruction set architectures, specifically RISC-V, are the primary beneficiaries of the legal conflict between two of the semiconductor sector’s largest partners. She rejected claims that RISC-V is capturing significant commercial market share from proprietary architectures in mainstream global markets.

According to Badani, RISC-V is not obtaining meaningful traction as an alternative processor architecture outside of China. She attributed its growth in China’s domestic market primarily to substantial state financial backing and direct government push, rather than organic commercial displacement of established instruction sets in international markets.

Her comments contrast with views from Qualcomm and prominent computer architecture researchers evaluating long-term hardware trends. Last week, Akeana, a U.S. semiconductor startup that designs processors using RISC-V architecture, was acquired by Qualcomm. Akeana’s CEO confirmed the acquisition in a LinkedIn post. 

Evolving AI requires more architectural freedom

As AI algorithms and models advance rapidly, chip designers need flexibility to modify processor cores, add specialized microarchitectural features, and improve overall energy efficiency.

“As AI is evolving, chip designers need total flexibility to adapt their cores with new functions and improve performance,” Mateo Valero, director of the Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC), told EE Times. “Relying on closed ISAs such as Arm limits the freedom and the possibility to implement new capabilities and improve power consumption. Even the largest companies using Arm’s IP with full architectural licenses have difficulties optimizing their designs due to Arm’s tight conditions and limited support. That’s why we believe that open standard ISAs such as RISC-V offer the best alternative.”

Ultimately, Arm views the $2 nominal damages award and the court’s reluctance to intervene in licensing negotiations as validation of its good-faith practices. However, the implications of the four-year legal battle extend far beyond the Wilmington courtroom. Although Arm and Qualcomm continue to collaborate on technical matters and product roadmaps, the legal friction highlights a pivotal juncture for chip designers.

data.title: Deepx Building Open Software Ecosystem to Scale Physical AI Beyond the Data Center
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

The next competitive battle in edge AI may not be decided by TOPS alone, according to Lokwon Kim, founder and CEO of Deepx, in an interview with EE Times Asia. The more consequential question, he said, is whether AI semiconductor companies can make their technology easy to develop, deploy, and scale.`

That does not make silicon less important. Kim’s view is that hardware remains the entry point, but software and ecosystem support determine whether a technical advantage becomes a sustainable commercial position.

Deepx has built its strategy around this distinction as it shifts from developing low-power AI accelerators to building a broader platform for physical AI. The company is connecting its neural processing units (NPUs) to existing model frameworks, development platforms, and embedded systems rather than building an entirely closed software stack.

The strategy reflects a broader challenge facing physical AI. Unlike cloud AI, where developers can often work within relatively standardized computing environments, physical AI must operate across cameras, robots, vehicles, drones, industrial equipment, and other systems with widely different power, thermal, sensor, operating-system, and real-time requirements.

For Deepx, that fragmentation has become one of the biggest barriers to moving AI projects beyond proof of concept.

“We see the physical AI semiconductor business developing in three stages. First, differentiated hardware performance must earn the customer’s initial selection. Second, a company must expand design wins and mass production, commercialize at scale, and build a defensible position through a strong portfolio of foundational IP. The third stage is to create an ecosystem in which developers can continuously build and deploy AI models and software using tools that are already familiar and broadly adopted,” Kim said.

Beyond the TOPS race

Edge AI hardware has traditionally been evaluated using metrics such as TOPS and performance per watt. Those measurements remain relevant, particularly in power-constrained systems, but they don’t capture the full requirements of physical AI.

For Deepx, the challenge is translating hardware performance into products that customers can develop and manufacture at scale.

The company points to Nvidia as an example of how a hardware advantage can become a much larger ecosystem advantage. Nvidia’s long-term differentiation has not depended solely on individual GPU generations’ performance. CUDA has created a development environment around the hardware, giving developers an established set of tools and workflows.

Physical AI, however, does not yet have an equivalent undisputed ecosystem leader.

“Physical AI semiconductors do not yet have an undisputed incumbent with that level of ecosystem dominance. That makes this period particularly important. Whoever succeeds in building an open developer ecosystem and establishing a de facto standard early can shape the market for years to come,” Kim said.

Deepx is therefore pursuing an open approach that connects its NPUs to ecosystems developers already know. Its collaborations include Ultralytics YOLO, Baidu PaddlePaddle, and Raspberry Pi, while the company is also working on support for Nvidia Isaac applications and other software environments.

The objective is straightforward: reduce how often developers have to rebuild their software as an AI application moves from experimentation to production.

Closing the PoC-to-production gap

For many physical AI projects, demonstrating that an AI model can run is only the first step. Production introduces a different set of engineering constraints.

A system must operate consistently across thousands or millions of units, meet a defined power budget, stay within thermal limits, support the required models, meet cost targets, and provide predictable long-term supply and software support.

Deepx identifies four major barriers between proof of concept and mass deployment: power and thermal constraints, model compatibility, total system cost, and production readiness.

Power is particularly unforgiving in physical AI. Cameras, drones, and robots cannot simply adopt data center-class processors and cooling systems. The processor must fit within the physical and thermal constraints of the product.

“The first is power and thermal constraints. Physical AI products such as cameras, robots, and drones cannot accommodate data-center-class power consumption or cooling systems. If power and heat exceed the physical limits of the product, no other advantage can compensate. This is a non-negotiable constraint,” Kim said.

Model compatibility creates another potential failure point. A semiconductor may show strong benchmark performance, but if converting and optimizing the customer’s models degrades accuracy or requires extensive software redevelopment, that advantage can disappear.

System cost is equally important. Customers evaluate the complete bill of materials rather than the NPU price in isolation. Memory, host processors, power management, cooling, and other components all contribute to whether an AI-enabled product can meet its commercial target.

Finally, production readiness requires more than a successful evaluation board. Customers need dependable supply, manufacturing yield, quality control, long-term software support, and evidence from actual production and field deployment.

That changes a semiconductor vendor’s role.

“A semiconductor vendor therefore cannot stop at supplying a chip and demonstrating performance. It must help the customer run the required models, reduce system-level power and cost, and work alongside them from software integration and pilot production through quality validation and volume manufacturing,” Kim said.

The implication is that the most important benchmark may ultimately be how quickly a customer can turn an AI model into a commercially viable product.

Portability becomes a design requirement

This is where software portability matters most.

Physical AI projects rarely start on the final production platform. Developers typically begin with a familiar model, a camera, and an accessible development board. Once the application is validated, the system must transition to industrial hardware.

That transition can introduce significant engineering work if the software environment changes with every hardware platform.

Deepx’s collaboration with Raspberry Pi aims to address this problem by providing developers with an accessible starting point and a path to industrial deployment. The company wants developers to be able to validate vision models and applications on familiar hardware before moving to industrial cameras, robots, gateways, and production systems using the same Deepx execution environment.

The company has identified three lessons from its early developer engagement. First, the entry point must be simple, with documentation, installation procedures, familiar workflows, and technical support carrying significant weight. Second, hardware decisions can be influenced during prototyping, well before production. Third, an easy development platform is not enough unless developers can carry their models and software into industrial validation and production.

That creates a different definition of portability. It is not simply about moving an application between two boards. It is about preserving the developer’s initial software investment throughout the product lifecycle.

An open stack for a fragmented market

Deepx does not expect physical AI to converge on a single software platform in the same way Android became a dominant smartphone operating system.

A robot’s hardware and operating requirements are fundamentally different from those of a camera, vehicle, drone, or medical device. Instead, Kim expects the industry to converge around multiple de facto standards at different layers of the stack.

PyTorch, Ultralytics, and PaddlePaddle are positioned around model development; ExecuTorch can support lightweight edge deployment; llama.cpp is becoming relevant for generative AI; and ROS 2 and Nvidia Isaac provide important assets for robotics development.

“The central question is not who owns every layer of the stack. It is who can connect different models, frameworks, and hardware platforms to actual silicon and production products with the least friction. Developers will not accept having to rewrite their software for every new processor,” Kim said.

The company’s objective is not to own every layer of software. Instead, it wants its NPU and execution environment to become a common hardware foundation across several ecosystems.

Distributors become engineering partners

Deepx’s ecosystem strategy also extends into its distribution network.

As it began mass production of its first commercial product, the company established partnerships with 27 distributors, including Avnet, WPG, Macnica, and DigiKey, as well as regional partners across several markets.

Kim argues that the role of a semiconductor distributor has changed as AI moves into industrial applications. Distribution is no longer limited to inventory, logistics, and sales. Partners increasingly provide technical support, identify customers, engage in engineering, and support design-in activity.

Different applications also require different channels. Robotics, machine vision, factory automation, security, and healthcare have distinct procurement structures and technical-support requirements.

Intelligent vision as the first mass market

Among physical AI applications, intelligent vision appears closest to large-scale commercialization.

The reason is partly the size of the installed base. Security, video surveillance, transportation, retail, factory monitoring, and machine vision already have extensive camera deployments, while the AI models used in many of these applications are comparatively mature.

There is also a relatively direct economic case. AI can automate continuous video monitoring or visual inspection, reduce labor requirements, and identify incidents or defects faster. Importantly, companies can often add an edge AI processor without replacing the entire camera or infrastructure.

Smart manufacturing is another near-term opportunity. Asia-Pacific’s position within global manufacturing and electronics supply chains, combined with labor shortages and pressure to improve quality, is driving adoption in machine-vision inspection, worker safety, predictive maintenance, and logistics automation.

Robotics may eventually represent the largest physical AI market, but it is also considerably more difficult.

A vision system primarily needs to perceive and analyze. A robot must perceive its environment, decide, and execute physical action in real time. An incorrect perception can therefore become an incorrect movement or a safety event.

This raises the requirements for reliability, model robustness and system integration.

Kim identifies real-world model reliability, power and thermal constraints, system cost, software compatibility, connectivity and safety as the major remaining barriers. Physical AI models must maintain performance despite changes in lighting, vibration, weather, camera angles, and obstacles.

The resulting architecture cannot depend entirely on cloud connectivity. A robot or industrial machine must keep making immediate decisions when network connectivity is lost, or cloud responses are delayed. Data privacy can also keep sensitive industrial or personal information on the device.

For these reasons, on-device inference is an architectural requirement, not merely an alternative to cloud computing.

From edge AI to Federated AI

In Kim’s view, the next stage of physical AI development will require something resembling MLOps for distributed devices.

Cloud AI benefited from mature workflows that connect model training, deployment, monitoring, and updates. Physical AI remains much more fragmented, with deployment and operational management often handled independently for individual devices and projects.

That model will not scale when AI is deployed across millions of cameras, robots, and industrial machines.

Kim identifies five requirements: secure cloud-device communication; a reliable fleet-wide model; software deployment with rollback mechanisms; simple tools for managing field equipment; and unified monitoring of device status, performance, power, errors, and model accuracy.

Deepx describes the resulting architecture as “Federated AI,” while distinguishing it from federated learning.

Under this model, the data center handles training and centralized management, edge devices perform inference and control where latency, security, and energy efficiency matter, and gateways connect the two where necessary.

The company is working with AWS IoT Greengrass toward an environment where models trained in the data center can be securely deployed to devices, run locally on Deepx NPUs, and managed centrally as a fleet.

The significance is less about moving all AI out of the cloud than about dividing workloads where computation makes the most sense.

Physical AI as infrastructure

That division matters more as AI infrastructure hits physical constraints.

Kim points to the growing gap between the pace of AI model development and the time required to build data centers and energy infrastructure. AI models can advance in months, while new power capacity and large data-center projects take years to build.

He argues this mismatch will push more inference to the edge.

Deepx’s internal analysis compares data center GPU systems with on-device AI systems across power, servers, cooling, and network resources. The company says it found potential for about a 100-fold improvement in resource efficiency in some applications and system configurations.

The company is also examining whether increasingly capable models can operate within low-power devices. In an internal architecture-level simulation involving a 100-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model, with approximately 10% of parameters active at any one time, Deepx identified the potential for a single 5-W-class AI accelerator to generate more than 10 tokens per second. The company notes that the 5-W figure applies to the chip itself, while total system power varies with memory capacity, configuration, and operating conditions.

Deepx’s workload research further suggests that models at or below the 100-billion-parameter class could potentially handle more than 80% of inference requests in the physical AI scenarios it is targeting. Under that scenario, the data center would handle the remaining, more complex workloads, potentially allowing existing central infrastructure to serve more users or devices.

These figures are not presented as universal benchmarks. They illustrate the architectural leverage that becomes possible as more inference moves onto devices.

That is the central idea behind Deepx’s vision of physical AI as infrastructure.

The data center will continue to train frontier models and process the most demanding workloads. But cameras, robots, vehicles, drones, industrial equipment, and personal devices can increasingly perform inference locally.

In this architecture, billions of devices stop being simple endpoints waiting for instructions from centralized infrastructure. They become distributed computing nodes.

The next computing layer

Kim sees the transition as analogous to the move from desktop computing to mobile computing.

Low-power CPUs moved computation into handheld devices, creating a new mobility-focused computing model. Deepx expects ultra-low-power AI semiconductors to make a similar transition possible for AI, moving inference from centralized data centers into the machines and objects operating in the physical world.

The company describes this emerging class of devices as “Free-Token Machines”—not because token generation is literally free, but because local inference can occur without a data-center charge for every interaction and without continuous dependence on network connectivity.

The concept extends beyond inference. As models become capable enough and power-efficient enough to run locally, cameras, robots, and industrial systems can become agentic machines that perceive their surroundings, make decisions, and act.

That does not eliminate data centers. It changes what they are responsible for.

The cloud remains the center of frontier-model training and large-scale computation, while local devices absorb workloads where latency, privacy, power efficiency, and connectivity make centralized processing less practical.

The competitive question for edge AI is therefore broader than which NPU delivers the most TOPS per watt.

The question is whether an AI semiconductor platform can make the entire journey—from model development and prototyping to deployment, fleet management, and production—so straightforward that physical AI becomes repeatable at scale.

Everspin Technologies is looking to expand its magnetoresistive random-access memory (MRAM) beyond established industrial applications into AI servers, data centers, and satellite systems, as AI workloads increase demand for faster, persistent memory.

Everspin president and CEO Sanjeev Aggarwal sees the technology as a way to address limitations in existing memory. “If you care for performance, I think that MRAM is the only solution we have,” he told EE Times in an exclusive interview.

Aggarwal claimed that customers are considering MRAM both for its performance and reliability and because they have been unable to obtain some NOR flash products. A TrendForce report estimated that NOR flash contract prices rose by a cumulative 100% to 120% in the first half of 2026. It stated that AI-related demand consumed much of the limited supply, and NOR flash was among the first products to experience longer lead times and allocation. The report also mentioned that suppliers have not announced significant capacity expansion.

Aggarwal said sees an opportunity for MRAM to fill up the gap created by the NOR flash shortages, and that opportunity could amount to $3 billion in 2028 or 2029. He said Everspin has been developing a product for this market using TSMC’s manufacturing process.

“Now people cannot buy NOR flash,” he said. “Most of the fabs in Asia have converted from NOR flash to DRAM. Much better profit margins. Then what is the alternative? MRAM is the only alternative for standalone or discrete products. And that is where they approach us.”

He said MRAM had previously cost about three times as much as NOR flash, but the price difference had narrowed to about 1.5 times as NOR flash prices rose amid supply constraints.

“If you are going to use two NOR flash chips, you might as well just use one MRAM and be more cost-effective,” he said.

The economics depend on the application, including the number of chips required and the performance and reliability specifications. Aggarwal said Everspin’s distributors had begun requesting cross-reference information to help customers identify MRAM alternatives when particular NOR flash components were unavailable.

He added that other non-volatile memory technologies could also be unsuitable for some applications. Ferroelectric RAM (FRAM), for example, has lower available densities in the products he described, while non-volatile static random-access memory (NVSRAM) can present tradeoffs in reliability and operating conditions.

Everspin specifies an operating temperature range of minus 40°C to 125°C for the parts Aggarwal discussed. He cited reliability, SRAM- and DRAM-like performance, and read-write endurance as reasons customers select MRAM.

Everspin reported revenue of $55.2 million for 2025, up 9.5% from $50.4 million in 2024, according to its annual report filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Aggarwal said he expects the company to double revenue over three to four years, with the NOR flash opportunity and demand from data centers, aerospace and defense, low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites, and industrial automation contributing to its growth ambitions.

CXL demonstration explores MRAM’s role in AI memory

At the Storage Networking Industry Association (SNIA) Developer Conference in Santa Clara, California, Everspin demonstrated MRAM modules combined with a Compute Express Link (CXL) controller. The setup created a pool of persistent memory accessible through CXL.mem, a protocol that allows a system to access memory over a CXL connection.

Aggarwal said the demonstration was intended to show how MRAM could function as an additional memory tier between dynamic random-access memory (DRAM), which serves as working memory, and NAND flash, which provides storage. DRAM operates on a timescale of nanoseconds, while NAND flash access can take hundreds of microseconds, according to Aggarwal. Moving data between processing and slower storage can delay workloads.

“Our memory is 20 to 30 nanoseconds,” he said. “You can use it for storage as well as compute, reducing the gap between NAND storage and DRAM working memory.”

The proposed role for MRAM is to hold data generated during AI processing before transferring it to longer-term storage. Aggarwal said this could include key-value (KV) caches, checkpoints, and data awaiting a write to storage. A KV cache retains information that an AI model reuses while generating a response; checkpoints allow a computing job to resume after a failure.

MRAM’s capacity remains a limitation. Everspin’s densities currently reach one gigabit, although Aggarwal said devices could potentially be stacked to provide 8 Gb or 16 Gb. He argued that the technology would not need to match NAND flash capacity if it held intermediate data only temporarily.

The company is also developing a roadmap for higher-density memory and newer interfaces. Everspin has supplied IBM’s FlashCore Modules, Aggarwal said, and wants to expand its data center business with products that go beyond its existing DDR4 interface.

“Our demonstration of the CXL protocol with our existing DDR4 chip will start getting us some entry into the data center market,” he said. “And by the time we have a good foothold, we will have a 4-Gb DDR6 part ready to go right behind it.” Aggarwal estimated that this development would take about three years.

At the edge, Aggarwal said, MRAM could reduce the need to transfer data between devices and central servers for processing. He cited OpenMV as an example of an application in which Everspin has replaced SRAM and added MRAM for configuration.

Satellite deployment of MRAM

Earlier this year, Astro Digital selected Everspin’s 64Mb PERSYST spin-transfer torque MRAM (STT-MRAM), part number EM064LXQADG13IS1T, as the primary fail-safe memory for the boot process on its Raven satellite bus for a geosynchronous Earth orbit (GEO) mission. Boot memory stores the code needed to start a spacecraft’s electronics and support system recovery.

“What Astro Digital did recently was, they took our part and sent it into geosynchronous orbit,” Aggarwal said. “So, not low Earth, but they sent those to geosynchronous orbit.”

He said MRAM’s radiation tolerance is useful in space, while adding that the surrounding silicon can still be vulnerable to radiation damage. In the satellite configuration he described, a backup memory provides an additional safeguard if the surrounding circuitry is affected.

Aggarwal also cited MRAM’s write speed and reliability as advantages over NOR flash in satellite applications. He said the memory can be written almost three orders of magnitude faster than NOR flash and consumes less power in the applications he described.

Everspin lists 64-Mb, 128-Mb, and 256-Mb capacities in its PERSYST family, which uses a quad serial peripheral interface (QSPI).

Aggarwal also gave a general example of how MRAM could reduce chip count in some applications, but the comparison should not be read as a description of Astro Digital’s actual satellite configuration.

Exploring AI server workloads

The company has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with MaxLinear to evaluate MRAM alongside MaxLinear’s storage compression, encryption, and hardware acceleration platform for AI servers. The MoU will focus on metadata management, log data, write buffering, cache, and other data-intensive workloads.

The companies also plan technical validation and market development aimed at hyperscale cloud providers, AI infrastructure developers, and enterprise server customers. The agreement includes potential longer-term manufacturing, supply, and commercialization opportunities.

Aggarwal said MaxLinear was the first target for the work because of its accelerator technology. “They have accelerators, so they were very interested in the technology,” he said. “We are working with them to find the first use case.”

The MoU establishes an evaluation framework; it does not announce a finished product or a volume commitment.

Manufacturing expansion and supply

Everspin produces two main MRAM families: field-switched, or toggle, MRAM, and STT-MRAM. It manufactures toggle MRAM at its 8-inch facility in Chandler, Arizona. The company’s portfolio ranges from 128 kilobits to 1 Gb, spanning several densities and interfaces. Aggarwal said the company had shipped more than 200 million units over 20 years, with only a handful of returns.

Earlier this year, the company signed an initial 10-year foundry services agreement with Microchip Technology to establish an 8-inch MRAM and tunnelling magnetoresistance (TMR) sensor manufacturing line at Microchip’s Fab 4 facility in Gresham, Oregon. The agreement is intended to provide a second U.S. manufacturing source for toggle MRAM. The U.S. SEC filing stated that the first products are expected to ship in the second half of 2027.

“We signed a foundry services agreement with Microchip, which allows me to manufacture twice the amount of toggle MRAM that I could manufacture in Chandler,” Aggarwal said.

The agreement is also connected to a $40 million U.S. government contract awarded through Amentum Services, with Everspin acting as a subcontractor. Aggarwal said the work will qualify Everspin’s process at Microchip and provide the government with access to the company’s intellectual property and a second manufacturing line for future government products.

For STT-MRAM, Everspin has worked with GlobalFoundries on 12-inch wafers since 2016. It also plans to tape out a product using TSMC’s 16-nm process, which Aggarwal said would diversify supply.

The company’s aim is to have two manufacturing sources for both product families: Chandler and Oregon for toggle MRAM, and GlobalFoundries and TSMC for STT-MRAM. Aggarwal said capacity was not currently a constraint.

Everspin also faces competition in the commercial MRAM market. South Korean company Netsol, which uses Samsung Foundry, offers a 16-Mb product, Aggarwal said. He expects a 1-Gb product from the competitor to reach the market in 2028 or 2029.

India offers opportunities in aerospace, automotive, and rail

India is another potential market, particularly in aerospace and defense, electric vehicles, and railways. Aggarwal said he was seeking connections with the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), and Indian satellite companies.

He also identified battery management systems and vehicle data recorders as possible applications, alongside flight control systems. Everspin is working to expand its Indian distribution network. Aggarwal said the company was exploring local partnerships, including discussions involving Indian distributors and possible outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) arrangements.

Aggarwal said the company was also speaking with Indian automotive groups and exploring opportunities in rail. He cited existing deployments in rail systems in Europe, Japan, and China, where memory stores operational data.

“We are always in discussions about these potential opportunities,” he said of Indian railway opportunities. “There is nothing that I can talk about openly, but obviously the conversations are ongoing.”

For now, Everspin’s challenge is to turn MRAM’s performance and reliability advantages into broader adoption across these markets. Aggarwal expects demand to grow as manufacturing efficiencies reduce cost per bit.

data.title: India’s OSAT Buildout Puts Semiconductor Testing in Focus
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

With five semiconductor plants in India now in commercial production, the harder question is no longer if the country can package chips, but whether it can test them fast enough, across enough device types, to hit production targets.

The testing challenge arrives as global semiconductor test equipment sales are forecasted to grow 31% to $15.3 billion in 2026, following 55.3% growth in 2025, according to SEMI’s July 2026 forecast. The industry body expects sales to reach $20.8 billion by 2028, driven partly by increasing device complexity and more demanding performance and reliability requirements.

Against that backdrop, Indian outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) companies must accommodate different device types, meet production targets, and maintain test coverage as they scale. Some must modernize legacy testing platforms, while others need to develop test architectures from scratch for new chips.

Testing times

When an Indian chip facility announces it can produce 15 million chips a year, that number says little about how many testers it needs. A chip tested in under a minute and one that takes five to 10 minutes can demand very different amounts of equipment for the same output.

In September 2025, Emerson announced a partnership with Kaynes Semicon to deploy its NI Semiconductor Test System (STS) as the primary test platform across Kaynes’ OSAT facility in Sanand, Gujarat. EE Times spoke with Karthik Balasekar, chief business manager for semiconductor and electronics, and Ved Mahanta, principal account manager, both at NI India, part of Emerson.

“Customers typically conduct tester qualification before making a final purchasing decision,” Mahanta said. “The process generally takes six months to one year. In the case of Kaynes, we can publicly state that the company has decided to proceed with NI testers. We are in the process of delivering the testers in the coming months.”

Mahanta added that discussions with other OSAT facilities were ongoing, with many still qualifying test equipment. NI could not identify some of these companies because their engagements were not publicly disclosed.

Balasekar said the number of testers also depends on the time required to test each device and the production target. “Facilities handling millions of devices may need fewer testers if each test takes less than a minute,” he explained. “Testing complex chips that require five or 10 minutes per device could demand more equipment to meet the same production target.”

Mahanta said, “An OSAT might announce an annual capacity of 14 million or 15 million chips, for example. Such figures generally represent the combined output capacity of its production lines, whether the facility operates 10 lines, 50 lines, or another number.”

Mahanta said NI Emerson has not publicly announced a specific number of test systems for Kaynes. He compared OSAT capacity announcements with those of automotive plants, which state how many vehicles they can produce annually. “Actual production depends on customer demand,” he said.

For relatively simple chips, pin count and the types of tests required are key factors. A chip with fewer pins and simpler testing requirements takes less time to test, allowing the same number of testers to process more devices.

In production environments, the priority is to test as many chips as possible in the shortest time while ensuring that devices meet their required specifications.

Mahanta said TestStand, NI’s test automation platform, automates test sequences to speed up decisions on whether a batch of chips is suitable for delivery.

Balasekar indicated that Kaynes’s selection reflects the need for test platforms that can accommodate different semiconductor device types. “Our STS is a platform that supports both mixed-signal and RF applications,” he said. “For example, if Kaynes tests mixed-signal products today and moves to RF products later, it can reuse the same STS tester for different devices under test.”

Flexibility is only part of the picture. The test architecture that an OSAT needs also depends on whether it is handling an established chip or a new design. “Typically, customers want to test two types of devices: legacy devices and new products, commonly referred to as new product development,” Mahanta said.

For legacy products, manufacturers may rely on older test platforms that can no longer deliver the required throughput. “OSATs need to move these products to newer systems without compromising test coverage,” Mahanta said, adding that customers often do much of the preparatory work and specify what the OSAT needs to test.

New designs present a different challenge, particularly when the customer is a semiconductor startup. “Some Indian startups developing their own chips have never performed final testing and depend on the OSAT to guide them,” Mahanta said. “The OSAT must help determine how to test each device reliably and quickly enough to meet production and time-to-market requirements.”

Although new devices do not carry the technical debt associated with legacy test platforms, they may require the OSAT to develop a test architecture from scratch. “This includes determining the test requirements, selecting an appropriate system, and ensuring that it meets test coverage and throughput targets,” Mahanta said. “Such a system could come from NI Emerson or another test equipment supplier.”

Both challenges—migrating established products to newer test platforms and developing test architectures for new devices—become more difficult to address with increasing design complexity, Balasekar said.

As semiconductor devices gain functionality, OSATs will need test systems that can accommodate evolving requirements without compromising existing test coverage. Mahanta said modular PXI (PCI eXtensions for Instrumentation) systems can allow customers to add modules for new tests without changing existing test parameters. “Customers can expand their testing capabilities as their requirements evolve,” he said.

AI enters test development

For new devices, NI applies AI to parts of test development, including the initial design of test architectures.

Mahanta said an engineer could upload a chip’s datasheet to NI’s Nigel AI test development tool, which examines selected parameters and suggest a potential test architecture. “The engineer could then use the suggested framework as a starting point rather than developing the entire architecture from scratch,” he explained.

“This approach targets part of the work involved in test development, rather than replacing the validation engineer,” Mahanta said. “AI could take on some repetitive tasks, leaving engineers to focus on more complex problem-solving.”

Under India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 (ISM 2.0), the government will focus on building an ecosystem across six areas, including advanced packaging and testing units and talent, Ashwini Vaishnaw, India’s minister for electronics and information technology, said at SEMICON India 2026. For OSATs, that makes test system flexibility, device qualification, and the ability to accommodate different device requirements relevant to the industry’s next phase of growth.

Mahanta said NI has invested in local engineering capabilities so its engineers can support OSAT customers on site, reducing the need to bring specialists from Taiwan and Singapore. He also cited Tessolve, an NI partner serving customers globally, as an example of an Indian company participating in the testing ecosystem.

“There are integrated device manufacturers that base 40% to 50% of their product lines in India,” he said. “Building engineering expertise will be essential for Indian companies seeking to serve global semiconductor manufacturers.”

Balasekar said growth in OSATs and electronics manufacturing could outpace the availability of skilled workers. India’s exports of electronic devices and its expanding mobile phone manufacturing base add to the demand for talent. He pointed to the workforce development component of ISM 2.0 as one way to address the gap. “I think that will help India grow faster and keep pace with the market’s expansion,” he said.

data.title: Edge AI MCU Features Multimodal Compute, Tiered Memory
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Microcontrollers, going through nonstop evolution, have reached their next inflection point: edge AI. A new MCU takes cloud-based models and brings them into the traditional MCU landscape to make sense of edge AI.

Unlike conventional MCUs constrained by limited on-chip memory and compute, Synaptics said its Astra SR200 Series MCUs combine heterogeneous, AI-native compute and acceleration with integrated high-bandwidth custom DRAM scalable to hundreds of megabytes. This enables larger AI models and richer multimodal workloads to run entirely on the device.

At Synaptics Tech Day held in San Jose on Oct. 20, 2026, CEO Rahul Patel called SR200 an xMCU because it offers multiple compute dimensions on a single piece of silicon. He also called Synaptics a processor company at the edge.

John Weil, VP and GM for IoT and Edge AI Processor Business at Synaptics, called SR200 a new class of microcontrollers. He pointed to three fundamental tenets that enable this design transition. “Synaptics went down this path to enable edge AI-capable devices with always-on low-power modes and a greater compute envelope found in entry-level microprocessor units,” he said.

Edge AI-tailored compute

SR200, the industry’s first pairing of the Arm Cortex-M85 and the Cortex-M52 cores, combines high-performance compute with up to 400 GOPS of AI acceleration, 256 MB of custom DRAM, vision and audio capabilities, and hardware-rooted security. The edge AI MCU incorporates Synaptics’s Torq NPU and Google Research’s Coral NPU to power CNN and transformer workloads.

Synaptics brings a variety of Arm cores from an ultra-low-power domain to a high-performance domain,” Weil said. “This allows engineers to pick exactly the compute level they want.” That, along with SR200’s tiered memory architecture, is crucial for combining modalities such as voice, vision, audio, motion and contextual sensing, and responding to them in real time.

“We have put a lot of time and effort into bringing high-performance and efficient compute to a low price point and low power point,” Weil said. “But we also invested heavily in memory architectures that were designed to feed CPUs and NPUs more efficiently.”

Multi-tiered memory

Memory architectures are traditionally designed to feed the CPUs and NPUs. However, a closer look at many AI applications shows they typically aren’t even pushing the compute element; instead, they are pushing the memory interface hard.

This is why the amount of memory that’s being procured and put into the cloud infrastructure is huge. In a traditional microcontroller, we used to have hundreds of kilobytes of memory. Then it became common to have megabytes of memory. And now we are referring to things in hundreds of megabytes of memory.

SR200’s tiered memory architecture builds high-performance compute around an on-chip memory architecture. It also includes a custom DRAM interface with in-package memory, bringing HBM-like high-performance memory to a microcontroller.

This tiered memory architecture solves two problems. First, it feeds compute cores efficiently. Second, this appropriate amount of memory supports ultra-low-power, always-on AI processing. The memory is custom-designed to handle processing for applications such as always-on listening and respond to them simultaneously.

“In this memory-constrained world that we live in right now, it offers design engineers the potential to build really differentiated edge AI devices,” Weil said. “No one else is talking about MCUs having this level of tiered memory architecture and going into the hundreds of megabytes of capacity.”

Fine-tuned power consumption

The SR200 microcontrollers blend high-performance compute with low-power consumption. That’s critical for developing battery-powered edge devices. The tiered memory architecture also plays a key role in enabling ultra-low-power operation. Moreover, if you feed the neural processors more efficiently, you can also reduce the power consumption of the device, Weil added.

The SR200 microcontrollers are available in three pin-compatible tiers. SR210 delivers 200 GOPS for power-optimized, always-on voice and sensing. SR230 adds vision, display, and optional audio at 300 GOPS for mainstream multimodal devices. SR250 delivers 400 GOPS with dual vision and display paths for demanding edge applications.

These MCUs are designed for the next generation of AI wearables, battery-powered sensing devices, connected cameras, streamers, and industrial vision and voice systems. According to Weil, their biggest traction so far is in body-worn electronics.

data.title: Innovasea Packs Long-Life Electronics into Fish Tags
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Innovasea’s efforts to shrink its embedded system are not simply a packaging exercise. The Canadian company’s devices must be light enough for a fish to carry without materially changing its behavior, yet contain the electronics and battery needed to transmit useful data from underwater. The result is a design problem in which mass, power consumption, and reliability constrain one another.

The Bedford, Nova Scotia-based company develops acoustic telemetry equipment for researchers studying fish movement and behavior. Miniature transmitters travel with the animals; receivers detect their signals.

But that straightforward interaction depends on an engineering effort spanning firmware, acoustic transducers, sensing, and long-duration operation. Jean Quirion, Innovasea’s VP of research and development for fish tracking, describes a business whose products must meet biological requirements as carefully as electrical ones.

“Our customers who are biologists and scientists who are studying these things have rules about the proportion, the weight of the tag, and how that needs to be in proportion to the weight of the fish,” he said in an interview with EE Times. “It’s really not so much about the size; it’s about the actual mass of the tag that needs to be as little as possible.”

That distinction gives miniaturization a specific purpose: allowing researchers to study smaller animals without making the tracking equipment itself an undue influence on what they observe.

Designing around the battery

Innovasea’s smallest tag measures approximately 3 mm in diameter and 15 mm in length and weighs 0.3 g. Within that envelope are a battery, a microcontroller, transmission electronics, and a piezoelectric ceramic transducer.

The engineering challenge is not just fitting those elements together. It is making their limited energy supply support a useful deployment. More efficient microcontrollers help, but Quirion attributes much of the company’s capability to system-level optimization rather than component improvements alone. Firmware and electronics must work together to limit energy consumption while meeting the application’s transmission and sensing requirements.

“A huge core competency that we have is our ability to squeeze every nanoamp out of a battery and make the best possible use out of it so that their systems last as long as possible and similarly pack as much electronics as we can in a really, really small space,” Quirion said.

The tradeoffs vary across the product range. A tiny tag intended for a small fish has different constraints from a larger transmitter used to track sharks. The same engineering disciplines must accommodate both, without treating minimum size as the only measure of success.

The tags can also carry temperature and pressure measurements, adding environmental context to movement data. Innovasea has developed a proprietary predation sensor to identify another event that could otherwise complicate interpretation: a tagged fish being eaten.

“It has the ability to detect a state where the fish is now in the stomach of another fish,” Quirion said.

That capability makes the transmitter more than a location marker. It helps researchers distinguish an animal’s movements from those of a predator carrying its tag.

Reliability beyond the lab

Deployment life introduces another set of requirements. Some Innovasea receivers have been designed for continuous underwater operation for more than 10 years, and its largest shark-tracking tag targets a similar operating life. These specifications place reliability alongside size and energy efficiency as a central design objective.

“Reliability over a very long operating life is really, really important in everything that we do,” Quirion said.

Meeting that objective involves more than sealing electronics against water. Component selection, firmware robustness, power management, verification, validation, and real-world testing all contribute to a system expected to function through prolonged exposure to demanding conditions.

Innovasea manufactures the equipment in Bedford and ships it internationally, linking its engineering work directly to product delivery. Its immediate market remains fish research, although Quirion sees broader uses.

“It is really asset tracking in a sense,” he said. “In our world and in our application, these assets are fish that we are tracking, but it could be something else.”

data.title: How Singapore Connects Chip Research, Startups, and Manufacturing
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

As competition in the semiconductor industry expands beyond conventional process scaling to encompass photonics, power devices, advanced packaging, and heterogeneous integration, Singapore leverages its established R&D and manufacturing base to explore ways to bring deep tech to market.

Singapore is advancing technologies including advanced packaging, silicon photonics, power electronics, RF GaN, piezoMEMS, flat optics, and IC design. A pathway from research through technology translation to startups and industrial commercialization is gradually taking shape. Research platforms such as the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR) play a key role in connecting research outcomes with industry needs.

Three examples illustrate this journey: silicon carbide (SiC) power device research at A*STAR’s Institute of Microelectronics (A*STAR IME); metalens technology being commercialized by Singapore-based startup MetaOptics; and silicon photonics foundry Advanced Micro Foundry (AMF), which emerged from A*STAR’s technology translation efforts before being acquired by GlobalFoundries. Together, they show how deep-tech innovations can progress from research and technology translation to industrial scale.

SiC research: from device development to technology translation

Chien Yu-Chieh (Jack), a senior scientist at A*STAR IME originally from Taiwan, focuses on SiC power MOSFETs, including device structures, process development, electrical characterization, and reliability. He aims to take his research beyond device development toward technology translation.

SiC is already an established material for commercial power semiconductors, but next-generation devices still face significant technical challenges. Chien noted, for example, that trench MOSFETs can reduce on-resistance but introduce challenges related to gate oxide integrity, defects at the SiC/SiO₂ interface, and long-term reliability.

Chien is therefore working on next-generation SiC device structures and fabrication processes. Because device design, fabrication, measurement, and reliability testing require repeated validation, access to a comprehensive research platform with the necessary equipment and cross-disciplinary expertise is critical. At A*STAR IME, he said, researchers can conduct device design, process development, and electrical characterization within the same R&D environment, shortening development cycles.

For Chien, the next step is to advance his research toward technology translation, potentially by establish a startup to turn the results into commercial applications and valuable IP.

MetaOptics: from metalens research to manufacturing

Founded in 2021 and headquartered in Singapore, MetaOptics specializes in manufacturing metalenses on glass substrates. Its technology uses nanoscale structures to directly control light waves, enabling thin optical elements to perform some of the functions traditionally achieved with multiple conventional lenses.

MetaOptics applies semiconductor manufacturing techniques to form nanoscale pillar structures on 12-inch glass wafers. By incorporating processes such as deep ultraviolet (DUV) immersion lithography, the company is advancing wafer-level metalens manufacturing. The approach could help shrink optical modules for smartphone cameras, wearables, machine vision, and other sensing systems.

For MetaOptics CEO  Aloysius Chua, the real challenge is not simply demonstrating that a metalens can form an image, but convincing customers that the technology works in real-world applications. For a deep-tech startup, developing a prototype is only the beginning. As Chua put it, “I need to show customers that my lens is working.”

Chua said MetaOptics must also complete customer validation and address process consistency, yield, and manufacturing scale. As nanoscale structures, optical design, and semiconductor lithography move toward volume production, process control becomes a key determinant of commercial competitiveness. A*STAR provides research resources and an R&D environment to help technologies bridge the gap between laboratory development and industrial applications.

AMF: scaling silicon photonics for industry

While MetaOptics and Chien’s work remain at the startup or technology validation stage, AMF offers a concrete example of deep tech advancing toward industrial-scale operations.

AMF is a Singapore-based silicon photonics foundry that grew out of A*STAR’s technology translation efforts. It operates a 200-mm manufacturing platform and provides silicon photonics prototyping, fabrication, and testing services. In November 2025, GlobalFoundries announced its acquisition of AMF, bringing the foundry’s manufacturing capabilities, silicon photonics IP, and talent into its global operations. GlobalFoundries said AMF was expected to contribute more than $75 million in revenue in 2026, helping the company target more than $1 billion in annual silicon photonics revenue by the end of the decade.

For GlobalFoundries, the acquisition brings more than a silicon photonics manufacturing platform. It adds AMF’s accumulated expertise, IP, and talent to the company. Yew Kong Tan, senior VP of GlobalFoundries APAC Manufacturing and general manager of the Singapore site, said the company’s silicon photonics collaboration with A*STAR dates back to 2015. The acquisition also creates an opportunity to bring 300-mm silicon photonics capabilities developed in the U.S. to Singapore, complementing A*STAR’s research capabilities.

“The acquisition actually allows us to combine capabilities on both sides,” Tan said. “From the research technology standpoint, AMF’s talent can also support 300-mm research. At the same time, the acquisition allows us to expand the capacity that the market needs in Singapore.”

GlobalFoundries also announced plans to establish a silicon photonics R&D center of excellence in Singapore in collaboration with A*STAR. The work will include developing next-generation silicon photonics technologies and materials for data transmission at 400 Gbps. GlobalFoundries plans to use AMF’s existing 200-mm platform to serve markets such as long-haul optical communications, computing, LiDARs, and sensing, with the potential to expand to 300-mm manufacturing as demand grows.

AMF illustrates another critical stage in deep-tech commercialization. Once research has been taken up by a startup and validated in the market, further growth requires an established manufacturing platform, accumulated expertise, and IP. Integrating these assets into a larger semiconductor company can extend the technology’s reach and expand its market potential.

A*STAR: bridging research and industry

This is the essence of what Yeo Yee Chia, A*STAR’s assistant chief executive for innovation and enterprise, calls “technology translation.” He emphasized that research institutions must go beyond conducting research: They need to work backward from industry needs to determine which equipment, talent, and technical capabilities to build.

This kind of platform support is particularly important for deep tech. Metalenses require nanoscale fabrication and wafer-level manufacturing; SiC power devices need device design, process development, and reliability validation; and silicon photonics involves optical devices, CMOS-compatible processes, wafer fabrication, packaging, and testing. These technologies often require years of capital-intensive R&D, while initial market demand may be too limited to justify a startup investing in a full set of production tools or building a complete R&D team on its own.

As Yeo noted, the value of a research institution extends beyond publishing academic papers or filing patents. More importantly, it lies in establishing the infrastructure and capabilities needed to validate, refine, and commercialize emerging technologies. For startups, this can lower early-stage barriers by allowing them to access research and development resources without bearing the full upfront capital expenditure. For larger enterprises, it provides access to technology platforms, IP, and expertise that have already progressed through technical validation and are better positioned for industrial deployment.

data.title: Chris Lattner: AI Code Generation Doesn’t Solve Software Engineering
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

For AI chip companies, the promise of AI-based coding agents is compelling: generate the low-level kernels needed to get a model running on new hardware, optimize them for performance, and do it without the software engineering resources traditionally required.

But according to Chris Lattner, CEO of AI software startup Modular (recently acquired by Qualcomm, where he now serves as executive VP of software engineering), chip companies should be wary of the limits of AI code generation. Making a kernel run fast is a very different problem from building software infrastructure we can depend on, he told EE Times in an exclusive interview.

“Agents are good, but they’re like anything else; it’s a tool, and you have to use it the right way,” Lattner said. “What I’ve seen with agents is they make tons of throwaway code. So, if you’re building a product, you don’t want to agent-generate everything.”

Agentic code generation makes sense for projects that are well-defined and limited in scope (e.g., “make this kernel go fast”), which can be quantified, measured, and validated, Lattner said, but bigger projects require product design and software engineering and can’t be delegated to agents.

“If you’re a startup and you only care about getting one model working, or getting it to go fast, [then go ahead,] use AI tools to prove it’s possible,” he said. “But that’s not going to be great for when you want to sell your chip to someone else, and they want to run a model you don’t have access to.”

Lattner said that despite some high-profile companies’ performance claims for their AI-generated low-level software, there are still many unanswered questions, including the dollar cost to generate large amounts of code and its applicability to large, open-ended problems.  

“I have heard of hardware companies that say they don’t believe in software anymore; they just want to use agents to generate everything,” Lattner said. “I think that’s interesting because they’re definitely using LLVM and still investing in compilers, but saying they’re not. So there’s a divergence between the party line and what’s actually happening.”

Writing performant low-level code for new and novel hardware has long been a difficult task for chip companies, and some are now relying on agents for this.

“Various people use [agentic code generation] as a talking point, particularly when their software is known to be problematic,” Lattner said. “So, I don’t really know what to believe in all these cases… great claims need great proof.”

Porting code

While AI is useful in some use cases, it can’t be used for everything, Lattner said. AI might help get a demo up and running, but this isn’t the same as writing a usable software stack with determinism and adaptability.

“The hard part about building a company or building a product or building something meaningful in the world is understanding the product requirements,” he said. “What is the marketing story? What is the product-market fit that you have to get for your product? I think that remains quite hard.”

At Modular, teams use agentic code generation for tasks such as porting PyTorch code into the company’s Max AI framework and for porting CUDA code to its programming language Mojo. Lattner said that porting code is a great use case for AI, along with specializing existing software (for example, specializing a matmul kernel for a specific size of matrix), since the agent can do this quickly and efficiently.

People will always need to know how to code, he said, since prompting in English isn’t precise enough to get a good result. 

“It’s true things are changing very rapidly—I use AI to write code, and I wouldn’t go back, personally—but that doesn’t mean that writing code was the job,” he said. “If you go back five years, more code was read than written.”

Open source under pressure

The downsides to AI code generation are still making themselves apparent in the world of software. Lattner identified open-source projects, the backbone of much of modern software, as being particularly under threat.

“Open-source projects like LLVM are under assault,” he said.

Before generative AI, people who wanted to contribute to open-source projects were motivated by the satisfaction of identifying and fixing problems, most often because they were using the software themselves and wanted to contribute. Making changes meant they had to invest a certain amount of time. Maintainers, people who had been working on the project for a long time, reviewed contributions for quality and worked with the community to teach them the nuances of the codebase. Lattner said the investment in teaching contributors improved the code.

“Today, that model is broken, because people are just vibe coding tons of patches and sending them to tons of projects, and the maintainers are getting completely overwhelmed with AI crap,” he said.

The deluge of AI-generated code is increasing the workload for maintainers, who have to review and iterate code before accepting it, Lattner said.

“And then the submitter doesn’t actually care, so the investment back into the human doesn’t lead to a future maintainer; it leads to someone who walks away, or just sets up their agents to spam a bunch of different projects to try to get GitHub badges,” he said. “This is a huge issue, so a lot of projects have stopped accepting contributions.”

The response from open-source projects such as LLVM has been to consider working only with established contributors, a move Lattner described as “terrifying.”

“The value of open-source projects is the humans, it’s the relationships, it’s the tribal knowledge,” he said. “If you destroy that, there’s going to be a huge problem… Running an open-source project and making it successful has always been super hard, so this is another pretty big threat.”

This is a huge challenge for all open-source projects today.

Modular’s programming language, Mojo, was recently open-sourced, but contributions aren’t yet being accepted. Lattner said the company intends to open to submissions gradually.

“It’s not just about the lines of code; it’s about the social side of things—if you have an employee that’s investing their effort into someone else, traditionally the thought would be, we’re investing in you, and if you’re good we’ll hire you, or [something might come out of it],” he said.

Things will stabilize, Lattner said. AI code review tools will improve, easing some of the burden, but ultimately, code review is difficult to automate completely because it requires judgement.

“What you’re building doesn’t just need to pass a test; it needs to be able to support the architecture we need for tomorrow and the future,” he said. “Models tomorrow will be better and faster, but I think these are inherent structural problems.”

Max alliance

For startups without the resources to build a state-of-the-art software stack, Lattner is planning on opening up Max, Modular’s AI framework, by starting an alliance for hardware makers. The alliance is planned to kick off around the end of the year, he said.

“This will be a big deal,” Lattner said. “We’re saying to everyone who has chips: You now have software. A lot of startups have been asking for help, but we always had to say no; we couldn’t scale to support them. Now we’ll be able to say yes, you can do it for yourself.”

Coding agents can solve for a specific kernel for a specific chip, but today’s complex, disaggregated, heterogeneous data center needs orchestration, scaling, and management, all of which must be handled by software, Lattner said.

“We’ve been building this for four and a half years—now you’ll be able to use it and scale it for yourself,” he said.

This is part of Qualcomm’s plan for Modular, Lattner said.

“[Qualcomm] wants it to be an open ecosystem so [its data center chip] can compete on its own merits,” he said. “Qualcomm is modest enough to understand it can’t [overtake Nvidia]. There will be a lot of different players with great contributions in different parts of the value chain, but it needs to be an open ecosystem.”

The Max alliance will enable edge chip companies and markets such as China, which Lattner is looking forward to.

“This is going to be very, very fun and exciting,” he said.
